title: Hello, C++
summary: The anatomy of a C++ program: #include, main, cout, and compile-then-run.
body:
Every C++ program starts running in a function called `main`. Here is the
smallest useful one:

```cpp
#include <iostream>    // brings in cout and cin
using namespace std;   // lets us write cout instead of std::cout

int main() {
    cout << "Hello, world!" << "\n";
    return 0;          // 0 means "everything went fine"
}
```

Line by line:

- `#include <iostream>` pulls in the input/output library. C++ has very little
  built in: almost every feature lives in a **header** that you include.
- `int main()` is the entry point. Unlike Python, loose statements outside a
  function are not allowed; execution begins at the top of `main`.
- `cout << x` sends `x` to standard output. Chain as many `<<` as you like.
  Nothing is added automatically: no spaces, no newline. `"\n"` ends the line.
- Every statement ends with `;`, and blocks live inside `{ }`. Indentation is
  only for humans.

**Compile, then run.** Python reads your file and runs it straight away. C++ is
first translated by a **compiler** (clang++ or g++) into a native program, and
only then executed:

```text
clang++ -std=c++17 hello.cpp -o hello   # 1. compile
./hello                                  # 2. run
```

CodeQuest does both steps for you. If the compiler finds a mistake, **nothing
runs** and you get a compile error instead. A forgotten `;` gives something
like `error: expected ';' after expression` along with a line number. Always
fix the **first** error first: later ones are often just follow-on noise.

title: Reading Input with cin
summary: cin >> reads typed values; getline reads whole lines.
body:
In C++ a variable must be **declared with a type** before you can store
anything in it. Then `cin >>` reads the next value from standard input and
converts it to that type:

```cpp
int age;
cin >> age;          // reads e.g. "42" and stores the number 42
```

`cin >>` skips any whitespace (spaces, tabs, newlines) and then reads one
**token**. It does not care about line breaks, so chaining works whether the
numbers are on one line or several:

```cpp
int a, b;
cin >> a >> b;       // "6 7" or "6\n7": both work
```

Python's `input()` works one *line* at a time, and you convert with `int()`.
In C++ the conversion comes from the variable's type: reading into an `int`
parses a number, and reading into a `string` grabs one word.

**Whole lines.** To read a line that contains spaces, use `getline` from
`<string>`:

```cpp
string full;
getline(cin, full);  // "Ada Lovelace"
```

**Pitfall:** `cin >> n` leaves the newline after the number unread. A
`getline` straight after it returns an empty string! Skip the leftover
whitespace with `cin >> ws` before calling `getline`.

**Reading until the input runs out:** `while (cin >> x) { ... }` keeps going
as long as a value was read successfully.

title: Comments, std:: and Compiler Errors
summary: Comments, namespaces, endl vs \n, headers, and how to read an error message.
body:
**Comments** come in two flavours:

```cpp
// a line comment, like Python's #
/* a block comment
   that can span lines */
```

**Namespaces.** Everything in the standard library lives inside the namespace
`std`, so its full name is `std::cout`, `std::string`, and so on.
`using namespace std;` lets you drop the prefix. That is fine for small
programs like ours. In big projects people prefer writing `std::`, because it
avoids name clashes.

**`endl` vs `"\n"`.** Both end a line, but `endl` also *flushes* the output
buffer, which is slow when you print many lines. Use `"\n"`.

**Include what you use.** Each library feature needs its own header:
`<iostream>` (cin/cout), `<string>`, `<vector>`, `<algorithm>`, `<cmath>`.
You will see `#include <bits/stdc++.h>` in competitive code. That is a
GCC-only shortcut that includes everything. CodeQuest ships a stand-in so it
works here too, but explicit headers are portable and compile faster.

**Reading compiler errors.** The two errors you will meet most often:

- `use of undeclared identifier 'cout'` (clang) or `'cout' was not declared`
  (gcc) means a missing `#include`, a missing `std::`, or a typo.
- `expected ';'` means you forgot a semicolon, usually at the **end of the
  previous line**, not the line that is reported.

The compiler checks types too. `int x = "hello";` is rejected before your
program ever runs, while Python would only complain once that line executed.

title: Variables & Types
summary: int, long long, double, char, bool, string, and why overflow bites.
body:
C++ is **statically typed**: every variable has a fixed type, chosen when you
declare it. In Python `x = 5` followed by `x = "hi"` is fine. In C++ the
second assignment is a compile error.

| type | holds | example |
|---|---|---|
| `int` | whole numbers, about ±2.1·10⁹ | `int n = 42;` |
| `long long` | whole numbers, about ±9.2·10¹⁸ | `long long big = 5'000'000'000;` |
| `double` | decimals (~15 significant digits) | `double pi = 3.14159;` |
| `char` | one character, in **single** quotes | `char c = 'A';` |
| `bool` | `true` / `false` (prints as 1 / 0) | `bool ok = true;` |
| `string` | text, in **double** quotes (`<string>`) | `string s = "hi";` |

**Overflow.** Python integers grow forever, but an `int` has a fixed 32 bits.
If a result goes past about 2.1 billion, signed overflow is *undefined
behaviour*. In practice you usually get a silently wrong, often negative,
number. The rule of thumb: **if a value can exceed ~2·10⁹, use `long long`.**

A classic trap is that the type of the *result variable* does not help:

```cpp
int a = 100000, b = 100000;
long long p = a * b;        // WRONG: a * b is computed as int, then stored
long long q = 1LL * a * b;  // right: the multiplication happens in long long
```

**Always initialise.** `int x;` without a value contains whatever garbage was
in memory, not 0 as you might expect. Write `int x = 0;`.

title: Arithmetic & Casts
summary: Integer division, %, mixing int and double, and static_cast.
body:
The operators look familiar (`+ - * / %`), but **the types decide the result**.

**Integer division truncates.** If both sides are integers, `/` throws away
the fractional part, so `7 / 2` is `3`. There is no separate `//` operator as
in Python. The truncation goes *toward zero*, which differs from Python for
negative numbers:

| expression | C++ | Python |
|---|---|---|
| `7 / 2` | `3` | `3.5` (`7 // 2` is `3`) |
| `-7 / 2` | `-3` | `-7 // 2` is `-4` |
| `-7 % 2` | `-1` | `1` |

To get a non-negative remainder in C++, write `((a % m) + m) % m`.

**Mixing types.** If either operand is a `double`, the whole operation is done
in `double`: `7 / 2.0` is `3.5`. To divide two `int` variables exactly,
**cast** one of them:

```cpp
int sum = 7, count = 2;
double avg = static_cast<double>(sum) / count;   // 3.5
double bad = sum / count;                         // 3 (already truncated!)
```

`static_cast<T>(x)` is the modern, explicit way to convert. The C-style form
`(double)sum` also works. Converting a `double` to an `int` truncates:
`static_cast<int>(3.99)` is `3`.

**Order matters** with integer division: `c * 9 / 5` and `9 / 5 * c` differ,
because `9 / 5` is already `1`.

Integer division or `%` by zero crashes the program (SIGFPE). Python would
raise `ZeroDivisionError` instead.

title: const, auto & Shortcuts
summary: Constants the compiler enforces, type deduction with auto, and += / ++.
body:
**`const`** marks a value that must never change. The compiler enforces this,
so it is more than a naming convention like Python's `MAX_SIZE`:

```cpp
const int MAX_N = 100000;
MAX_N = 5;   // error: cannot assign to variable 'MAX_N' with const-qualified type
```

`constexpr` goes further: the value is computed at **compile time**, so you
can use it, for example, as an array size.

**`auto`** asks the compiler to deduce the type from the initial value:

```cpp
auto n = 5;        // int
auto x = 5.0;      // double
auto big = 5LL;    // long long (LL suffix)
auto s = "hi";     // careful: const char*, NOT std::string
```

`auto` is not dynamic typing. The variable still gets one fixed type, which
you just do not have to spell out. It shines with long type names you will
meet later (`auto it = m.begin();`). For plain numbers, an explicit type is
often clearer.

**Shortcuts** (identical in spirit to Python, plus `++`/`--`):

```cpp
x += 3;   x -= 1;   x *= 2;   x /= 4;   x %= 7;
i++;      // add 1 (Python has no ++)
i--;      // subtract 1
```

`++i` (pre-increment) and `i++` (post-increment) differ only when you use the
value in the same expression. Keep `++` on its own line and you never have to
care.

title: Formatting Output
summary: fixed, setprecision, setw and setfill from <iomanip>.
body:
By default `cout` prints a `double` with **6 significant digits**, which
surprises Python users:

```cpp
cout << 3.14159265;   // 3.14159
cout << 1234567.0;    // 1.23457e+06  (!)
```

To control the digits, include `<iomanip>`:

```cpp
cout << fixed << setprecision(2) << 3.14159;   // 3.14
```

- `fixed` switches to plain decimal notation. With it, `setprecision(n)` means
  **n digits after the decimal point**, like Python's `f"{x:.2f}"`.
- Without `fixed`, `setprecision(n)` means n *significant* digits.
- Both settings are **sticky**: they stay in effect for everything printed
  afterwards.

For widths and padding:

```cpp
cout << setw(5) << 42;                      // "   42" (right-aligned, width 5)
cout << setfill('0') << setw(2) << 7;       // "07"
```

`setw` is the odd one out: it applies to the **next item only**, while
`setfill` is sticky.

If you know C, `printf("%.2f\n", x);` from `<cstdio>` works too. Just don't mix
it with `cout` after you have turned on fast I/O (you will meet that in a
later lesson).

Judges usually compare decimals with a tolerance, but when a problem says
"exactly two decimals", `fixed << setprecision(2)` is the tool.

title: switch
summary: Branch on an integer or char value, and beware of fall-through.
body:
When you compare **one integer or `char` value** against several constants,
`switch` is tidier than a chain of `else if`:

```cpp
switch (op) {
    case '+': cout << a + b; break;
    case '-': cout << a - b; break;
    case 'x':
    case '*': cout << a * b; break;   // two labels share one body
    default:  cout << "unknown";       // like a final else
}
```

**Always end a case with `break`.** Without it, execution *falls through*
into the next case's code. That is occasionally intended (as with `'x'` and
`'*'` above), but usually it is a bug. Python's `match` has no fall-through,
so this one catches Python programmers.

Rules the compiler enforces:

- The value must be an integer type, a `char`, or an `enum`. A **`string`
  does not work**: `switch (s)` fails with an error like *statement requires
  expression of integer type*. Use `if / else if` for strings.
- Case labels must be **compile-time constants** (`case 3:`, `case 'a':`), not
  variables.
- Declaring a variable inside a case needs its own braces:
  `case 1: { int t = 5; ... break; }`. Otherwise you get the error *jump to
  case label crosses initialization*.

title: Writing Functions
summary: Return types, typed parameters, void, and declare-before-use.
body:
A C++ function states its **return type** and the **type of every
parameter**:

```cpp
int square(int x) {        // returns an int, takes an int
    return x * x;
}

void greet(string name) {  // void: returns nothing
    cout << "Hi " << name << "\n";
}
```

Compare this with Python's `def square(x):`. The types are not decoration:
calling `square("hi")` is a **compile error**, caught before the program
runs.

**Declare before use.** The compiler reads your file top to bottom. If `main`
calls `square` but `square` is defined *below* `main`, you get
`use of undeclared identifier 'square'`. You can fix that in two ways:

1. Define helper functions above `main` (the usual style for short programs).
2. Put a **prototype** (just the signature plus `;`) near the top, and the
   full definition anywhere below:

```cpp
bool isPrime(int n);       // prototype: "this exists, trust me"

int main() { cout << isPrime(7); }

bool isPrime(int n) { ... }   // definition
```

**Every path must return.** If a non-`void` function can reach its closing
`}` without hitting a `return`, the behaviour is undefined, and you may get
garbage or a crash. Compilers only *warn* about this, so check your branches
yourself.

Like Python, `return` exits the function immediately, which is handy for
early exits (`if (n < 2) return false;`). A `void` function can use a bare
`return;`.

title: Pass by Value vs Reference
summary: Copies, & references, and const & for big objects.
body:
By default C++ passes arguments **by value**: the function gets its own
*copy*, and changing that copy does not affect the caller.

```cpp
void addOne(int x) { x++; }      // modifies a copy
int n = 5; addOne(n);            // n is still 5
```

Put `&` after the type to pass **by reference**. The parameter then becomes
another name (an alias) for the caller's variable:

```cpp
void addOne(int& x) { x++; }     // modifies the original
int n = 5; addOne(n);            // n is now 6
```

That is how a C++ function can "return" several results: it writes them into
reference parameters. A classic example is `swap(a, b)`.

**How does this compare with Python?** In Python, passing a list lets the
function mutate it, but rebinding an `int` parameter never affects the
caller. In C++ *you* choose, per parameter, and that applies to every type:
an `int` can be modified by reference, and a `vector` is **copied** if you
pass it by value!

**`const &` for big read-only objects.** Copying a vector of a million
elements on each call is slow. Pass it as `const vector<int>& v`: no copy is
made, and `const` promises (enforced by the compiler) that the function will
not modify it.

Rules of thumb:

- small types (`int`, `double`, `char`): pass by value
- big things you only read (`string`, `vector`): pass by `const &`
- anything the function must change: pass by `&`

A reference parameter needs a real variable. `addOne(5)` with `int&` fails to
compile, because you cannot modify the literal 5.

title: Overloading & Default Arguments
summary: Several functions with one name, chosen by argument types.
body:
In Python, defining a second `def area(...)` replaces the first. In C++ you
can have **several functions with the same name**, as long as their parameter
lists differ. This is called **overloading**:

```cpp
int area(int side)         { return side * side; }   // square
int area(int w, int h)     { return w * h; }         // rectangle
double area(double r)      { return 3.14159 * r * r; } // circle
```

The compiler picks the version whose parameters best match the arguments:
`area(3)` calls the first, `area(3, 4)` calls the second, and `area(2.0)`
calls the third. This happens at **compile time**, so there is no runtime
cost.

Some limits:

- The return type alone does not count. `int f(int)` and `double f(int)`
  conflict, with an error like *functions that differ only in their return
  type cannot be overloaded*.
- **Ambiguity is an error.** With only `f(long)` and `f(double)`, the call
  `f(5)` is an `int` that converts equally well to both, and the compiler
  refuses to guess (*call to 'f' is ambiguous*).

**Default arguments** cover the simple case where you just want an optional
parameter, like Python's `def f(x, times=1)`:

```cpp
void repeat(string s, int times = 1);
repeat("hi");      // times = 1
repeat("hi", 3);   // times = 3
```

Defaults must come **last** in the parameter list. Put them in the prototype
(or the definition if there's no prototype), but not in both.

You've already used overloading without noticing: `cout <<` is overloaded for
`int`, `double`, `string`, `char`, and more.

title: Recursion
summary: Functions that call themselves: base cases, the call stack, and memoisation.
body:
A **recursive** function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller
version of it. There are always two parts:

1. a **base case** that answers directly, with no further calls
2. a **recursive case** that moves *closer* to the base case

```cpp
long long factorial(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return 1;            // base case
    return n * factorial(n - 1);     // smaller problem
}
```

Each call gets its own copy of the parameters on the **call stack**. If the
base case is missing or unreachable, the recursion never stops, and the stack
overflows with a crash (*segmentation fault*). Python would raise
`RecursionError` after about 1000 calls. C++ allows much deeper recursion
(often 10⁵ or more simple calls), but the limit is real, and on a phone it can
be smaller.

**Watch for repeated work.** Naive Fibonacci calls itself twice per level, so
`fib(45)` makes over a billion calls:

```cpp
long long fib(int n) { return n < 2 ? n : fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2); }
```

**Memoisation** stores each answer the first time it is computed. In C++ that
is usually a `vector` passed by reference (or a global), much like Python's
`@lru_cache`:

```cpp
long long fib(int n, vector<long long>& memo) {
    if (n < 2) return n;
    if (memo[n] != -1) return memo[n];
    return memo[n] = fib(n - 1, memo) + fib(n - 2, memo);
}
```

Euclid's algorithm is a short, elegant recursion for the greatest common
divisor: `gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b)`, with `gcd(a, 0) = a`. (C++17 also
offers `std::gcd` in `<numeric>`.)

title: std::vector
summary: C++'s resizable list: push_back, size, indexing and range-based for.
body:
`std::vector` (from `<vector>`) is the C++ counterpart of a Python list, with
one difference: **all elements have the same type**, which you write in angle
brackets.

```cpp
vector<int> v;              // empty
vector<int> w = {3, 1, 4};  // with values
vector<int> z(5);           // five zeros
vector<int> f(5, -1);       // five copies of -1
```

| Python | C++ |
|---|---|
| `v.append(x)` | `v.push_back(x)` |
| `len(v)` | `v.size()` |
| `v[i]` | `v[i]` (unchecked) or `v.at(i)` (checked) |
| `v[-1]` | `v.back()` |
| `v.pop()` | `v.pop_back()` (returns nothing!) |
| `not v` | `v.empty()` |

**Range-based for** loops over the elements, just like `for x in v:`. Add `&`
when you want to *modify* them:

```cpp
for (int x : v) cout << x << " ";   // x is a copy
for (int& x : v) x *= 2;            // x is the real element
```

**No safety net.** `v[10]` on a 3-element vector does not raise an
IndexError. It reads random memory: you may get garbage, a crash, or worse,
nothing visible at all. `v.at(10)` checks the index and throws an exception
instead, which is useful while debugging. Negative indices do not wrap
around.

**The unsigned trap.** `v.size()` returns an *unsigned* number, so on an
empty vector `v.size() - 1` is not -1 but about 1.8·10¹⁹. If you write
`for (int i = 0; i < (int)v.size() - 1; i++)`, the cast to `int` *before*
subtracting keeps you safe.

Reading `n` numbers into a vector:

```cpp
int n; cin >> n;
vector<int> a(n);
for (int& x : a) cin >> x;
```

title: std::string
summary: length, +, substr, find and npos, comparison, and getline.
body:
`std::string` (from `<string>`) is a sequence of `char`s. Unlike Python's
`str`, it is **mutable**: `s[0] = 'J';` simply changes the first letter.

| Python | C++ |
|---|---|
| `len(s)` | `s.size()` or `s.length()` |
| `s + t` | `s + t` (also `s += t`) |
| `s[i:i+k]` | `s.substr(i, k)` (start, **length**!) |
| `s[i:]` | `s.substr(i)` |
| `s.find(t)` | `s.find(t)` returns `string::npos` if absent |
| `t in s` | `s.find(t) != string::npos` |
| `str(42)` | `to_string(42)` |
| `int(s)` | `stoi(s)` / `stoll(s)` |

**`substr` takes a length, not an end index.** `s.substr(2, 3)` means "3
characters starting at index 2", whereas Python's `s[2:3]` is one character.
This is a very common slip.

**`npos`.** When `find` fails it does not return -1 but `string::npos`, a
huge unsigned value. Always compare with `npos`. To search again *after* a
match, pass a start position: `s.find(t, pos + 1)`.

**Comparing:** `==`, `<`, `>` work on whole strings, alphabetically by
character code. In that order uppercase letters come before lowercase ones.

**Literals are not strings.** `"ab" + "cd"` does not compile, because both
are plain C character arrays. Make at least one side a `string`:
`string("ab") + "cd"`.

`cin >> s` reads one **word**. Use `getline(cin, s)` for a whole line, and
remember the leftover-newline trap after `cin >>` (fix it with `cin >> ws`).

title: Characters & char Arithmetic
summary: chars are small numbers: 'a' + 1, c - '0', and <cctype> helpers.
body:
A `char` is really a **small integer**, namely the character's code (ASCII).
`'A'` is 65 and `'a'` is 97, and the letters and digits are consecutive. So
arithmetic works directly, with no `ord()` or `chr()` needed:

```cpp
char c = 'a' + 2;        // 'c'
int pos = 'e' - 'a';     // 4: the letter's index in the alphabet
int d = '7' - '0';       // 7: digit character to number
char up = c - 'a' + 'A'; // 'C'
```

`'a'` (single quotes) is a `char`, while `"a"` (double quotes) is a string.
They are not interchangeable: `s == 'a'` will not compile when `s` is a
string.

**Printing gotcha:** `cout << 'a' + 1` prints `98`, because `char + int` is
an `int`. Convert back to see the letter: `cout << char('a' + 1)`.

`<cctype>` has the usual tests and conversions:

```cpp
isdigit(c)  isalpha(c)  isupper(c)  islower(c)  isspace(c)
toupper(c)  tolower(c)          // these return int: wrap in char(...) to print
```

**Looping over a string** works like looping over a vector. Use `char&` to
change characters in place:

```cpp
for (char& ch : s) ch = toupper(ch);
```

**Wrapping around the alphabet** (Caesar cipher style) combines everything:
first get the index, then shift with `%`, and finally convert back.

```cpp
char shifted = 'a' + (c - 'a' + k) % 26;
```

A **counting array** is often simpler than a map for letters:
`int cnt[26] = {0}; cnt[c - 'a']++;`

title: pair, tuple & Structured Bindings
summary: Bundle values together, compare them lexicographically, and unpack them.
body:
`pair<A, B>` (from `<utility>`) holds two values, possibly of different types.
It is the C++ version of a 2-tuple:

```cpp
pair<string, int> p = {"Ada", 36};
cout << p.first << " " << p.second;   // Ada 36
auto q = make_pair(3, 4.5);           // pair<int, double>
```

**Pairs compare lexicographically**, just like Python tuples: first by
`.first`, and on a tie by `.second`. That makes `min`, `max` and sorting work
out of the box, and a trick like "sort by score, then by name" becomes
`pair<int, string>`.

`tuple` (from `<tuple>`) holds any number of values. You access them with
`get<index>`, and the index must be a compile-time constant:

```cpp
tuple<int, string, double> t = {1, "x", 2.5};
cout << get<1>(t);                    // x
```

**Structured bindings** (C++17) unpack them, much like `a, b = pair` in
Python:

```cpp
auto [name, age] = p;                 // copies
auto& [x, y] = p;                     // references: changes affect p
```

They also work in loops, which you will use constantly with maps:
`for (auto& [key, value] : m)`.

**When to use what?** `pair` is perfect for quick "two values" jobs such as
coordinates or (value, index). Once `.first` and `.second` stop being
obvious, a `struct` with real field names (coming in a later unit) reads
better. A `tuple` is handy for returning several values from a function:
`return {sum, mn, mx};`.

title: map & unordered_map
summary: Key-value dictionaries, counting with m[key]++, and the [] insertion trap.
body:
C++ has two dictionary types:

- `map<K, V>` (from `<map>`) keeps keys **sorted**, and each operation takes
  O(log n) time.
- `unordered_map<K, V>` (from `<unordered_map>`) is a hash table like
  Python's `dict`. It is O(1) on average, but iteration order is arbitrary.

```cpp
map<string, int> age;
age["Ada"] = 36;
age["Alan"] = 41;
cout << age["Ada"];
```

**Counting is a one-liner.** `m[key]` creates a missing key with value `0`,
so `cnt[word]++` works without the `dict.get(word, 0)` dance from Python.

**The trap:** `m[key]` *always* inserts when the key is absent, even when you
only meant to *look*. `if (m["bob"] > 0)` silently adds `"bob"` with value 0.
To test whether a key exists without inserting it, use:

```cpp
if (m.count(key)) ...                // 1 if present, 0 if not
auto it = m.find(key);               // m.end() if absent
if (it != m.end()) cout << it->second;
```

**Iterating** gives `pair<const K, V>` elements, which unpack nicely with
structured bindings. With a `map` they come out in sorted key order:

```cpp
for (const auto& [word, c] : cnt) cout << word << " " << c << "\n";
```

Remove a key with `m.erase(key)`, and get the number of keys with `m.size()`.

Which one should you pick? Use `map` when you need sorted output or ordered
queries. Otherwise use `unordered_map` for raw speed.

title: set & unordered_set
summary: Unique elements: insert, count, erase, and always-sorted iteration.
body:
A `set<T>` (from `<set>`) stores **unique** values, always in **sorted
order**. `unordered_set<T>` (from `<unordered_set>`) is the hash-based
version, closer to Python's `set`: faster on average, but unordered.

```cpp
set<int> s;
s.insert(5);
s.insert(1);
s.insert(5);            // already there: ignored
cout << s.size();       // 2
```

| Python | C++ |
|---|---|
| `s.add(x)` | `s.insert(x)` |
| `x in s` | `s.count(x)` (0 or 1) |
| `s.discard(x)` | `s.erase(x)` |
| `len(s)` | `s.size()` |
| `min(s)` / `max(s)` | `*s.begin()` / `*s.rbegin()` |

That last row shows a superpower of the ordered `set`: the smallest and
largest elements are always at hand, even as you keep inserting and erasing.
Python has no built-in equivalent. (The `*` *dereferences* an iterator, which
the next lessons explain.)

`insert` returns a pair whose `.second` says whether the value was new. That
is handy for "first time I've seen this?" checks:

```cpp
if (seen.insert(x).second) { /* x was new */ }
```

Building a set from a vector removes duplicates in one step:

```cpp
set<int> uniq(v.begin(), v.end());
```

`multiset<T>` allows duplicates while staying sorted. Careful there:
`ms.erase(x)` removes **all** copies of `x`. To remove one copy, use
`ms.erase(ms.find(x))`.

title: stack, queue & priority_queue
summary: LIFO, FIFO and always-the-largest-first containers.
body:
These three **container adapters** give you a deliberately small interface:

| | header | add | look | remove |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `stack<T>` (LIFO) | `<stack>` | `push(x)` | `top()` | `pop()` |
| `queue<T>` (FIFO) | `<queue>` | `push(x)` | `front()` | `pop()` |
| `priority_queue<T>` | `<queue>` | `push(x)` | `top()` | `pop()` |

**`pop()` returns nothing.** Python's `list.pop()` hands you the element, but
in C++ you read it first and then remove it:

```cpp
int x = st.top();
st.pop();
```

Calling `top()`, `front()` or `pop()` on an **empty** container is undefined
behaviour, usually a crash, so check `empty()` first.

**`priority_queue` is a max-heap**: `top()` is always the *largest* element.
Python's `heapq` is a *min*-heap. To get a min-heap in C++, pass the
`greater` comparator (from `<functional>`):

```cpp
priority_queue<int> maxHeap;
priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>> minHeap;
```

A common trick avoids the long type: push negated numbers into a max-heap.
Heaps of pairs order by `.first`, then `.second`, exactly like comparing
pairs.

Typical uses:

- **stack**: matching brackets, undo history, depth-first search
- **queue**: breadth-first search, simulations of a waiting line
- **priority_queue**: "always process the cheapest or most urgent next",
  as in Dijkstra's algorithm, scheduling, or keeping the top k values

Both `push` and `pop` on a heap are O(log n), and `top()` is O(1).

title: Iterators
summary: begin/end, *it and ++it, and lower_bound on sets and maps.
body:
An **iterator** is a position inside a container. It is what makes the
standard algorithms work the same way on vectors, strings, sets and maps.

```cpp
vector<int> v = {10, 20, 30};
auto it = v.begin();   // points at 10
cout << *it;           // * reads the element: 10
++it;                  // move to 20
```

- `c.begin()` is the first element.
- `c.end()` is **one past the last** element. It is not an element, so never
  dereference it.
- The range `[begin, end)` is half-open, like Python's `range(0, n)`.
- For a map, `it->first` and `it->second` reach the key and value
  (`it->x` is shorthand for `(*it).x`).

The range-based `for` is just this loop with the details hidden:

```cpp
for (auto it = v.begin(); it != v.end(); ++it) cout << *it << " ";
```

**Ordered containers can search for neighbours.** `s.lower_bound(x)` returns
an iterator to the first element `>= x`, and `s.upper_bound(x)` to the first
element `> x`. Both take O(log n), and you have to check them against
`s.end()`:

```cpp
auto it = s.lower_bound(x);
if (it != s.end()) cout << "next >= x is " << *it;
if (it != s.begin()) cout << "previous < x is " << *prev(it);
```

**Invalidation.** Changing a container can make existing iterators dangle.
After a `push_back`, old vector iterators may point at freed memory.
Erasing during a loop needs the iterator that `erase` returns:

```cpp
for (auto it = s.begin(); it != s.end(); )
    if (*it % 2) it = s.erase(it); else ++it;
```

title: Binary Search: lower_bound & upper_bound
summary: Search a sorted vector in O(log n) and count values in a range.
body:
On a **sorted** range, `<algorithm>` offers three O(log n) searches:

```cpp
binary_search(v.begin(), v.end(), x)   // bool: is x present?
lower_bound(v.begin(), v.end(), x)     // iterator to first element >= x
upper_bound(v.begin(), v.end(), x)     // iterator to first element >  x
```

These match Python's `bisect_left` and `bisect_right`, except that they
return **iterators**. Subtract `v.begin()` to turn one into an index:

```cpp
int idx = lower_bound(v.begin(), v.end(), x) - v.begin();
```

If every element is smaller than `x`, you get `v.end()`, which means index
`v.size()`. Check for that before reading `*it`.

Combining the two gives powerful one-liners:

```cpp
// how many copies of x?
upper_bound(v.begin(), v.end(), x) - lower_bound(v.begin(), v.end(), x)
// how many elements <= x?
upper_bound(v.begin(), v.end(), x) - v.begin()
// how many in [lo, hi]?
upper_bound(..., hi) - lower_bound(..., lo)
```

**The input must be sorted** (with the same ordering you search by). On
unsorted data these functions do not complain, they just return nonsense. So
sort once, then answer many queries quickly. That is the standard pattern
when `n` and the number of queries are both around 10⁵: a linear scan per
query would be 10¹⁰ steps, while binary search needs about 17 steps per
query.

For a `set` or `map`, use the member functions `s.lower_bound(x)` instead.
The free function works on them too, but it is O(n) there.

You can also binary-search on the *answer*: if a condition is false up to some
value and true after it, halve the range `lo..hi` in a loop. This is a
classic technique for optimisation problems.

title: The Algorithm Toolbox
summary: accumulate, min_element, max_element, count, reverse, unique and friends.
body:
Before you write a loop, check whether `<algorithm>` or `<numeric>` already
has it. These all take a `begin, end` range:

| Python | C++ | header |
|---|---|---|
| `sum(v)` | `accumulate(b, e, 0LL)` | `<numeric>` |
| `min(v)` / `max(v)` | `*min_element(b, e)` / `*max_element(b, e)` | `<algorithm>` |
| `v.index(min(v))` | `min_element(b, e) - b` | `<algorithm>` |
| `v.count(x)` | `count(b, e, x)` | `<algorithm>` |
| `v.reverse()` | `reverse(b, e)` | `<algorithm>` |
| `list(range(1, n+1))` | `iota(b, e, 1)` | `<numeric>` |
| `any(p(x) for x in v)` | `any_of(b, e, p)` | `<algorithm>` |

**The `accumulate` trap.** The type of the *initial value* decides the type
of the running total. `accumulate(v.begin(), v.end(), 0)` adds in `int` and
overflows on large sums, and `accumulate(..., 0)` over doubles truncates them
to integers! Pass `0LL` for big integer sums and `0.0` for doubles.

`min_element` and `max_element` return **iterators**: use `*` to get the
value, or subtract `v.begin()` to get its index. On an empty range they
return `end`, and dereferencing that is undefined.

**Removing duplicates** is a two-step idiom. First `sort`. Then `unique`
moves the distinct values to the front and returns the new logical end, and
`erase` chops off the leftovers:

```cpp
sort(v.begin(), v.end());
v.erase(unique(v.begin(), v.end()), v.end());
```

Some other gems: `next_permutation` steps through all orderings, `fill` sets
a range to one value, `count_if` counts with a predicate lambda, and for two
values `min(a, b)` / `max(a, b)` (or `max({a, b, c})` for several) do what
you'd expect.

title: Fast Input & Output
summary: sync_with_stdio(false), cin.tie(nullptr), and why endl is slow.
body:
By default `cin` and `cout` stay synchronised with C's `scanf` and `printf`,
and `cin` flushes `cout` before every read. That is safe, but slow: reading
10⁶ numbers can take longer than solving the problem. Two lines at the top of
`main` fix it:

```cpp
int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);  // stop syncing with C stdio
    cin.tie(nullptr);             // don't flush cout before each cin
    ...
}
```

You will see this in nearly every competitive C++ solution (and in
CodeQuest's starter code). It is the equivalent of switching from Python's
`input()` to `sys.stdin.readline`.

**Rules once you have done this:**

- **Don't mix** `cin`/`cout` with `scanf`/`printf`/`puts` any more. The two
  systems now buffer separately, so output can come out in the wrong order.
- **Use `"\n"`, not `endl`.** `endl` forces a flush every time, which throws
  away the benefit of buffering. Printing 10⁵ lines with `endl` can be several
  times slower.
- In an *interactive* program, where you must see output before the next
  input arrives, you need to flush explicitly with `cout.flush()` or `endl`.
  CodeQuest's problems are not interactive.

**Build output, then print.** For huge outputs it is fine to `cout <<`
inside a loop now, because the stream is buffered. There is no need to glue
a giant string together first, as you might in Python with `"\n".join(...)`.

**Watch the input size.** At 2·10⁵ numbers, each up to 10⁹, sums need
`long long`. Reading with `cin >> x` into the right type is still all you
need.

title: Pointers & References
summary: Addresses with &, dereferencing with *, nullptr, and how pointers differ from references.
body:
Every variable lives at some **address** in memory. A **pointer** is a
variable that stores such an address:

```cpp
int x = 10;
int* p = &x;     // &x = "address of x";  p points to x
cout << *p;      // *p = "the int p points to": 10
*p = 20;         // writes through the pointer: x is now 20
```

Note that the symbols do double duty. In a **declaration**, `int*` means
"pointer to int" and `int&` means "reference to int". In an **expression**,
`&x` takes an address and `*p` follows one (*dereferences* it).

**`nullptr`** means "points at nothing". Dereferencing a null pointer, or one
that points at memory which no longer exists, is undefined behaviour and
typically ends in a *segmentation fault*. Python has no such thing: every
name refers to a live object, or the lookup raises an error.

**Pointer vs reference:**

| | reference `int& r = x;` | pointer `int* p = &x;` |
|---|---|---|
| can be null? | no | yes (`nullptr`) |
| can be re-pointed? | no, bound forever | yes, `p = &y;` |
| syntax to use | just `r` | `*p`, or `p->field` |

So prefer references, and use a pointer when "nothing" is a valid answer,
for example a search that can fail, or an optional link in a linked list.

**Arrays and pointers.** A built-in array decays to a pointer to its first
element, and `p + i` steps `i` elements forward. That is how `v.data()` and
`begin()` work under the hood, and also why going out of bounds silently
reads neighbouring memory.

**Python intuition:** a Python variable is a bit like a pointer that is
dereferenced automatically and can never dangle. C++ makes the indirection
explicit, and leaves the safety to you.

title: Dynamic Memory & unique_ptr
summary: new/delete, leaks, RAII, and letting unique_ptr clean up for you.
body:
Local variables live on the **stack** and vanish automatically when their
scope ends. Sometimes an object must outlive the function that creates it,
or its size is only known at runtime. Then it goes on the **heap**:

```cpp
int* p = new int(42);   // allocate
cout << *p;
delete p;               // you MUST free it yourself
```

Python's garbage collector frees memory for you. With raw `new`/`delete`,
**you** are the garbage collector, and the classic bugs follow: forgetting
`delete` (a *leak*), deleting twice, or using memory after `delete` (a
*dangling pointer*).

**RAII** ("Resource Acquisition Is Initialisation") is C++'s answer: tie the
resource to an object whose **destructor** frees it automatically when the
object goes out of scope. You already rely on this, because `vector` and
`string` free their memory on their own.

For single heap objects, use **`unique_ptr`** from `<memory>`:

```cpp
auto p = make_unique<int>(42);   // owns the int
cout << *p;                      // use it like a pointer
// no delete: freed automatically when p goes out of scope
```

- A `unique_ptr` has exactly **one owner**. It cannot be copied (a compile
  error), only *moved*: `auto q = move(p);` transfers ownership, and leaves
  `p` null.
- `shared_ptr` (via `make_shared`) allows several owners and frees the object
  when the last one disappears. It is handy, but costlier, so reach for it
  only when ownership really is shared.

**Modern rule of thumb:** you should almost never write `new` or `delete`.
For many objects, use a `vector`. For one object with an owner, use
`unique_ptr`. For a linked structure, use nodes holding
`unique_ptr<Node> next`.

A *destructor* is written `~ClassName()` and runs automatically when the
object dies. That is the hook RAII builds on.

title: Common Pitfalls
summary: The bugs every C++ beginner meets, and how to spot them fast.
body:
C++ trusts you, so many mistakes compile fine and misbehave at runtime. Here
are the usual suspects, roughly in order of how often they bite:

1. **Uninitialised variables.** `int sum;` holds garbage, not 0. Always write
   `int sum = 0;`.
2. **`=` instead of `==`.** `if (x = 0)` assigns 0 and tests false, so the
   branch *never* runs and `x` is overwritten in the process.
3. **Signed overflow.** `int` stops at about 2.1·10⁹. Use `long long` for sums,
   products and anything that might grow, and write `1LL * a * b`.
4. **Integer division.** `sum / n` truncates before it is stored in a
   `double`. Use `static_cast<double>(sum) / n`.
5. **Out-of-bounds access.** `v[n]` on a vector of size `n`, or a loop with
   `i <= n`, reads memory that isn't yours, with no IndexError. Use `v.at(i)`
   while debugging.
6. **Unsigned underflow.** `v.size() - 1` on an empty vector is huge. Cast
   first: `(int)v.size() - 1`.
7. **`getline` after `cin >>`** returns an empty line. Use `cin >> ws`.
8. **Missing `return`** in a non-void function, or returning a reference to a
   local variable that is destroyed when the function ends.
9. **Copying big things** by value in function parameters or `for (auto x : v)`.
   Use `const auto&`.

**Undefined behaviour (UB)** is the real enemy. For bugs like 1, 3, 5 and 8
the C++ standard promises *nothing*. The program may work on your phone, fail
on the judge, or change behaviour when you add a `cout`. If output looks
"impossible", suspect UB first.

**Tools that help** on a desktop: compile with `-Wall -Wextra` to get warnings
about most of these, and `-fsanitize=address,undefined` to catch
out-of-bounds and overflow at runtime with a precise report.

`input()` reads **one line** of text from standard input and returns it as a
string (without the trailing newline).

applies a function to every piece:

title: Variables & Types
summary: Store values in names and learn the four basic types: int, float, str, bool.
body:
A **variable** is a name that points at a value. You create one with `=`
(read it as "becomes", not "equals"):

```python
score = 10        # int   - whole number
price = 4.99      # float - number with a decimal point
name = "Ada"      # str   - text
done = False      # bool  - True or False
```

Python figures out the type from the value. Ask for it with `type()`:

```python
print(type(score))   # <class 'int'>
```

A variable can be re-assigned at any time, even to a different type, and the
right-hand side is evaluated **first**, so `score = score + 1` means "take
the old score, add one, store it back".

### Converting between types

`int("42")`, `float("3.5")`, `str(7)` and `bool(0)` convert values. You need
this constantly, because **`input()` always returns a `str`**:

```python
a = input()        # the user types 12
print(a + a)       # 1212  - string concatenation!
print(int(a) + int(a))   # 24
```

> **Pitfall:** `"5" + 5` is a `TypeError`. Python never guesses whether you
> meant text or maths - convert explicitly.

Names are case-sensitive (`Score` and `score` differ), may contain letters,
digits and `_`, and cannot start with a digit. Prefer clear names like
`total_price` over `tp`.

title: Arithmetic Operators
summary: + - * / plus the three you will use all the time: //, % and **.
body:
Python has the usual operators, plus a few that are gold for programming
puzzles:

| Operator | Meaning | Example | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `/` | true division | `7 / 2` | `3.5` |
| `//` | floor division | `7 // 2` | `3` |
| `%` | remainder (modulo) | `7 % 2` | `1` |
| `**` | power | `2 ** 10` | `1024` |

> **Pitfall:** `/` **always** gives a float, even `6 / 3` is `2.0`. When you
> need a whole number (an index, a count) use `//`.

`//` and `%` are a pair: for any `a` and positive `b`,
`a == (a // b) * b + a % b`. That makes them perfect for splitting numbers:

```python
n = 1234
last_digit = n % 10      # 4
rest = n // 10           # 123
minutes, seconds = divmod(200, 60)   # 3, 20
```

`x % 2 == 0` tests "is x even?". `//` rounds **down** (towards minus
infinity), so `-7 // 2` is `-4`, not `-3`.

Precedence follows maths: `**` first, then `* / // %`, then `+ -`. Use
parentheses when in doubt: `(a + b) / 2`.

Python integers have **no size limit**: `2 ** 200` just works. Floats, on
the other hand, are approximations: `0.1 + 0.2` prints
`0.30000000000000004`. Never compare floats with `==`; check that the
difference is tiny instead.

Shortcut operators update a variable in place: `x += 3`, `x *= 2`, `x //= 10`.

title: f-strings & Formatting
summary: Build output text with f-strings, round numbers and control decimals.
body:
Gluing text with `+` and `str()` gets messy fast. An **f-string** (a string
with an `f` in front) lets you drop any expression straight into `{}`:

```python
name, age = "Ada", 36
print(f"{name} is {age} years old")
print(f"Next year: {age + 1}")
```

### Format specs

After a colon inside the braces you can say *how* to show the value:

```python
pi = 3.14159265
print(f"{pi:.2f}")      # 3.14     - 2 decimals
print(f"{42:5}|")       #    42|   - width 5, numbers right-aligned
print(f"{'ab':>5}|")    #    ab|   - right-align text
print(f"{1234567:,}")   # 1,234,567
print(f"{0.25:.0%}")    # 25%
```

`:.2f` is the one you will use most - many judges ask for "exactly two
decimal places".

### round()

`round(x, 2)` returns a *number* rounded to 2 places, while `f"{x:.2f}"`
returns *text* that always has 2 decimals. Note `round(2.5)` is `2`:
Python rounds halves to the nearest **even** number ("banker's rounding").
And `round(1.50, 2)` prints as `1.5` - if the output format matters, use an
f-string.

> **Pitfall:** forgetting the `f` prints the braces literally:
> `"{name}"` stays `{name}`.

title: if, elif, else
summary: Make decisions with comparisons and boolean logic.
body:
`if` runs a block only when a condition is `True`. The block is everything
**indented** under the line ending in `:` (use 4 spaces):

```python
temp = int(input())
if temp > 25:
    print("hot")
elif temp > 10:
    print("mild")
else:
    print("cold")
```

Python checks the conditions **top to bottom and stops at the first true
one**, so order matters: if the `> 10` test came first, 30 degrees would be
"mild".

### Comparisons

`==` equal, `!=` not equal, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`. They produce a `bool`.
Python allows chaining: `0 <= x < 10` means `0 <= x and x < 10`.

> **Pitfall:** `=` assigns, `==` compares. `if x = 5:` is a syntax error.

### Combining conditions

`and` (both true), `or` (at least one), `not` (flip):

```python
if age >= 13 and age <= 19:
    print("teen")
if not done:
    print("keep going")
```

`and`/`or` are *short-circuit*: in `x != 0 and 10 / x > 2` the division
never runs when `x` is 0.

Empty things are "falsy": `0`, `0.0`, `""`, `[]`, `None`. So `if name:`
means "if name is not empty".

> **Pitfall:** `if x == 1 or 2:` is always true (it reads as
> `(x == 1) or 2`). Write `if x == 1 or x == 2:` or `if x in (1, 2):`.

title: while Loops
summary: Repeat code as long as a condition stays true.
body:
A `while` loop repeats its block **while** a condition is true. It checks the
condition before every round:

```python
n = 3
while n > 0:
    print(n)
    n -= 1
print("go!")
```

Use `while` when you **don't know in advance** how many repetitions you
need - "keep halving until it reaches 1", "keep reading until the input is
0", "keep guessing until correct".

Every `while` loop needs three things:

1. a variable the condition depends on, set up **before** the loop,
2. the condition itself,
3. a line **inside** the loop that changes that variable.

> **Pitfall:** forget step 3 and the condition never becomes false - an
> **infinite loop**. In CodeQuest that shows up as "time limit exceeded".

A classic `while` example is the *Collatz* process: if `n` is even halve
it, otherwise make it `3n + 1`. Nobody has proven it always reaches 1, but
it does for every number ever tried:

```python
steps = 0
while n != 1:
    if n % 2 == 0:
        n //= 2
    else:
        n = 3 * n + 1
    steps += 1
```

Another common pattern is peeling digits off a number with `% 10` and
`// 10` until nothing is left (`while n > 0`).

examples.title: Countdown
examples.code:

    print(n)
    n -= 1
print("go!")
examples.explain: The condition is re-checked before each round; n -= 1 guarantees it ends.

examples.title: Digit sum
examples.code:

total = 0
while n > 0:
    total += n % 10
    n //= 10
print(total)
examples.explain: Each round removes the last digit, so the loop stops when n hits 0.

examples.title: Doubling until big
examples.code:
money = 1
days = 0
while money < 1000:
    money *= 2
    days += 1
print(days, "days ->", money)
examples.explain: We don't know the number of rounds up front - perfect for while.

title: for Loops & range
summary: Loop over sequences and count with range(start, stop, step).
body:
A `for` loop visits each item of a sequence in turn:

```python
for fruit in ["apple", "kiwi", "fig"]:
    print(fruit)
```

To repeat something a fixed number of times, loop over `range`:

```python
for i in range(5):        # 0 1 2 3 4
    print(i)
```

`range` has three forms:

- `range(stop)` - 0 up to **but not including** `stop`
- `range(start, stop)` - `start` up to `stop - 1`
- `range(start, stop, step)` - jumps by `step`; a negative step counts down

```python
range(1, 11)        # 1..10
range(0, 20, 5)     # 0 5 10 15
range(10, 0, -1)    # 10 9 ... 1
```

> **Pitfall (off-by-one):** the stop value is **excluded**. To include `n`
> write `range(1, n + 1)`. To count down to 1, the stop must be `0`.

Why exclude the end? Because `range(n)` then has exactly `n` items, and
`range(len(lst))` gives exactly the valid indexes of a list.

### Accumulators

Most loops build up an answer in a variable created *before* the loop:

```python
total = 0
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    total += i
```

Use `for` when you know what to iterate over; use `while` when you only
know when to stop.

print(list(range(2, 6)))

print(list(range(5, 0, -1)))
examples.explain: list(range(...)) is a quick way to see which numbers a range produces.

title: break & continue
summary: Leave a loop early or skip to the next round.
body:
Two keywords change how a loop flows:

- `break` - exit the loop **immediately**.
- `continue` - skip the rest of this round and jump to the **next** one.

```python
for n in range(1, 10):
    if n % 2 == 0:
        continue      # skip even numbers
    if n > 7:
        break         # stop completely
    print(n)          # 1 3 5 7
```

### The "loop until a sentinel" pattern

Often input ends with a special value such as `0`. Combine `while True`
with `break`:

```python
while True:
    x = int(input())
    if x == 0:
        break
    print(x * 2)
```

`while True` would run forever on its own; the `break` is the exit door.
This keeps the "read" and the "check" next to each other, instead of
duplicating `input()` before and inside the loop.

### for ... else

A loop can have an `else` block that runs only if the loop finished
**without** hitting `break`. It is handy for searches:

```python
for d in range(2, n):
    if n % d == 0:
        print("not prime")
        break
else:
    print("prime")
```

> **Pitfall:** `break` only leaves the **innermost** loop. To escape nested
> loops, use a flag variable or put the loops in a function and `return`.

Use these sparingly - a loop with many `break`s is hard to follow. But for
"stop at the first match" they make code shorter and faster.

examples.explain: Evens are skipped by continue; break ends the loop when n reaches 9.

    x = int(input())
    if x == 0:
        break
    count += 1
print("read", count, "numbers")
examples.explain: The sentinel 0 is not counted.

title: Indexing & Slicing
summary: Pick out characters and substrings with s[i] and s[a:b:step].
body:
A string is a **sequence** of characters, numbered from `0`:

```text
 s =   P   y   t   h   o   n
       0   1   2   3   4   5
      -6  -5  -4  -3  -2  -1
```

```python
s = "Python"
s[0]     # 'P'
s[-1]    # 'n'  - negative indexes count from the end
len(s)   # 6
```

The last valid index is `len(s) - 1`; `s[6]` raises `IndexError`.

### Slices

`s[a:b]` takes characters from index `a` **up to but not including** `b` -
the same rule as `range`. Leave a side empty to mean "from the start" or
"to the end":

```python
s[0:3]    # 'Pyt'
s[2:]     # 'thon'
s[:-1]    # 'Pytho'  - drop the last char
s[::2]    # 'Pto'    - every second char
s[::-1]   # 'nohtyP' - reversed!
```

Slices are forgiving: `s[2:100]` just stops at the end instead of raising
an error.

### Strings are immutable

You cannot change a string in place: `s[0] = "J"` is a `TypeError`.
Instead build a **new** string: `s = "J" + s[1:]`.

Why immutable? It makes strings safe to share and lets Python use them as
dictionary keys. The price: building a long string by repeated `+=` in a
loop is slow - collect pieces in a list and `"".join` them (next lesson).

A common trick: a word is a palindrome when `w == w[::-1]`.

print(len(s), s[len(s) - 1])
examples.explain: Index len(s) - 1 and index -1 both mean the last character.

examples.title: Slices

print(s[:3])
print(s[3:])
print(s[::2])
print(s[::-1])
examples.explain: s[:3] + s[3:] always rebuilds the original string.

s = "cat"
s = "b" + s[1:]
print(s)
try:
    s[0] = "r"
except TypeError as e:
    print("error:", e)
examples.explain: To 'change' a string, build a new one and re-assign the name.

title: String Methods
summary: upper, strip, find, replace, split and join - the everyday text toolkit.
body:
Strings come with dozens of **methods** - functions you call with a dot:

```python
s = "  Hello, World  "
s.strip()           # 'Hello, World'   - trim whitespace at both ends
s.lower()           # '  hello, world  '
s.upper()           # '  HELLO, WORLD  '
s.replace("l", "L") # '  HeLLo, WorLd  '
s.count("l")        # 3
s.find("World")     # 9  (index of first match, -1 if missing)
"World" in s        # True
s.strip().startswith("He")   # True
```

> **Pitfall:** strings are immutable, so methods **return a new string**.
> `s.upper()` on its own line does nothing useful - write `s = s.upper()`.

### split and join

These two are opposites and you will use them in nearly every problem:

```python
words = "red green  blue".split()      # ['red', 'green', 'blue']
"a,b,c".split(",")                     # ['a', 'b', 'c']
"-".join(["red", "green", "blue"])     # 'red-green-blue'
"".join(["a", "b", "c"])               # 'abc'
```

`split()` with **no argument** splits on any run of whitespace and ignores
leading/trailing spaces - usually what you want. `split(" ")` splits on
every single space and leaves empty strings when there are doubles.

`join` is called on the **separator**, and every item must already be a
string: `" ".join(map(str, numbers))` converts numbers first.

Handy checks: `isdigit()`, `isalpha()`, `isupper()`, `islower()`, `isspace()`.

Methods can be chained because each returns a string:
`input().strip().lower().replace(" ", "")`.

title: Characters, ord & chr
summary: Loop over characters and turn letters into numbers and back.
body:
Looping over a string gives you one character at a time:

```python
for ch in "Hi 5!":
    if ch.isalpha():
        print(ch, "is a letter")
    elif ch.isdigit():
        print(ch, "is a digit")
```

### Characters are numbers underneath

Every character has a code (its **Unicode code point**). `ord` gives the
number, `chr` goes back:

```python
ord("a")    # 97
ord("b")    # 98
chr(65)     # 'A'
```

Letters are consecutive, so arithmetic on codes is meaningful:

```python
pos = ord(ch) - ord("a")      # 'a' -> 0, 'b' -> 1, ... 'z' -> 25
ch = chr(ord("a") + pos)      # and back again
```

Write `ord("a")` rather than the magic number `97` - it documents your
intent and avoids mistakes.

### Wrapping around with %

To shift a letter by `k` places and wrap from `z` back to `a`, use modulo
26:

```python
new = chr((ord(ch) - ord("a") + k) % 26 + ord("a"))
```

This is the **Caesar cipher**, one of the oldest encryption schemes.

> **Pitfall:** the steps are *subtract `ord('a')`, add, `% 26`, add back*.
> Forgetting to subtract first means `% 26` is applied to 97..122 and the
> result is garbage. Also remember uppercase letters start at `ord("A")`
> (65).

Building the result: append each new character to a list and finish with
`"".join(chars)` - faster and cleaner than repeated `+=`.

for ch in text:
    if "a" <= ch <= "z":
        ch = chr((ord(ch) - ord("a") + 13) % 26 + ord("a"))
    out.append(ch)
print("".join(out))
examples.explain: Shifting by 13 twice brings you back - ROT13 is its own inverse.

title: Lists
summary: Ordered, changeable sequences: append, pop, len, slicing and sorting.
body:
A **list** holds many values in order, inside square brackets:

```python
nums = [5, 3, 8]
nums.append(1)      # [5, 3, 8, 1]   add at the end
nums[0] = 7         # [7, 3, 8, 1]   lists ARE mutable
last = nums.pop()   # removes and returns 1
nums.insert(0, 9)   # [9, 7, 3, 8]
len(nums)           # 4
8 in nums           # True
```

Indexing and slicing work exactly like strings: `nums[-1]`, `nums[1:3]`,
`nums[::-1]`. Useful built-ins: `sum`, `min`, `max`, `sorted`.

### Reading a list from input

```python
nums = list(map(int, input().split()))
```

### Sorting: sort() vs sorted()

- `nums.sort()` sorts **in place** and returns `None`.
- `sorted(nums)` returns a **new** sorted list and leaves `nums` alone.

Both accept `reverse=True`.

> **Pitfall:** `nums = nums.sort()` sets `nums` to `None`!

### Aliasing

Assignment never copies a list - it gives the *same* list a second name:

```python
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a          # same list
b.append(4)
print(a)       # [1, 2, 3, 4]  - surprise!
c = a.copy()   # or a[:] - a real copy
```

> **Pitfall:** `[[0] * 3] * 3` makes three references to *one* inner list.
> Build grids with `[[0] * 3 for _ in range(3)]` instead.

`pop()` from the end is fast; `pop(0)` from the front has to shift every
element, so it is slow for big lists (see `deque` later).

examples.code:

nums.append(1)
nums[0] = 7
print(nums, len(nums))
print("popped", nums.pop(), "->", nums)
nums.insert(0, 9)
print(nums, nums[1:3], sum(nums), max(nums))
examples.explain: append/pop work at the end; insert puts an item at a given index.

examples.title: sort vs sorted
examples.code:

print(sorted(nums), nums)
nums.sort(reverse=True)
print(nums)
print(nums.sort())
examples.explain: sorted() returns a copy; .sort() changes the list and returns None.

b = a
c = a.copy()
b.append(4)
print(a, b, c)

title: Tuples & Unpacking
summary: Fixed groups of values, multiple assignment and the a, b = b, a swap.
body:
A **tuple** is like a list that cannot change. Write it with parentheses
(or just commas):

```python
point = (3, 4)
rgb = 255, 128, 0     # parentheses optional
point[0]              # 3
```

Use a tuple for a fixed bundle of related values: a coordinate, a
`(name, score)` pair, a date. Being immutable, tuples can be dictionary keys
and set members - lists cannot.

> **Pitfall:** a one-item tuple needs a trailing comma: `(5,)`. Plain
> `(5)` is just the number 5 in brackets.

### Unpacking

Assign a sequence to several names at once:

```python
x, y = point                 # x = 3, y = 4
name, score = "Ada", 91
first, *rest = [1, 2, 3, 4]  # first = 1, rest = [2, 3, 4]
```

The counts must match (except for the starred name), otherwise you get
`ValueError: too many values to unpack`. That is also why
`a, b = map(int, input().split())` crashes when the line has three numbers.

Swapping needs no temporary variable:

```python
a, b = b, a
```

The right side builds a tuple *first*, then unpacks it.

### Comparing tuples

Tuples compare **element by element**, left to right, like words in a
dictionary: `(2, "b") < (2, "c") < (3, "a")`. This makes them perfect for
"sort by score, then by name". A trick for "highest score, ties by smallest
name": take `min` of `(-score, name)`.

Functions can return several values - they are really returning one tuple:
`return lo, hi`.

examples.code:

x, y = point
print(x, y, type(point))
first, *rest = [1, 2, 3, 4]
print(first, rest)
print(type((5)), type((5,)))
examples.explain: The trailing comma, not the parentheses, makes a tuple.

print(sorted(people))
negated = [(-91, "Bob"), (-85, "Ada"), (-91, "Al")]
print(min(negated))   # highest score, ties -> smallest name
print((2, "b") < (2, "c") < (3, "a"))
examples.explain: The first element decides; ties fall through to the next element.

title: Sets
summary: Unordered collections of unique items with lightning-fast membership tests.
body:
A **set** stores each value **at most once**, with no particular order:

```python
s = {3, 1, 3, 2}       # {1, 2, 3}
s.add(5)
s.discard(1)           # remove if present (no error if missing)
len(s)                 # 3
2 in s                 # True - and very fast
```

`set(some_list)` removes duplicates in one step, so
`len(set(words))` counts distinct words.

### Why sets are fast

`x in my_list` checks items one by one - slow for big lists. A set uses
**hashing** to jump straight to where `x` would be, so `x in my_set` takes
about the same time whether the set has 10 or 10 million items. If your
code does many `in` checks, convert to a set first.

### Set algebra

```python
a = {1, 2, 3, 4}
b = {3, 4, 5}
a | b     # union         {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}
a & b     # intersection  {3, 4}
a - b     # difference    {1, 2}
a ^ b     # in exactly one {1, 2, 5}
```

> **Pitfall:** `{}` is an empty **dict**, not a set. Write `set()`.

> **Pitfall:** sets have no order and no indexes - `s[0]` is an error, and
> printing a set may show items in any order. When output order matters,
> use `sorted(s)`.

Only immutable values can go in a set: numbers, strings, tuples - but not
lists. Sets themselves are mutable; `frozenset` is the immutable version.

examples.title: Unique values
examples.code:

uniq = set(words)
print(len(words), "words,", len(uniq), "distinct")
print(sorted(uniq))

examples.explain: sorted() turns the set into a list with a predictable order.

title: Dictionaries
summary: Map keys to values: lookup, .get, counting and looping with items().
body:
A **dictionary** maps **keys** to **values**, like a phone book:

```python
ages = {"Ada": 36, "Linus": 28}
ages["Grace"] = 45        # add or overwrite
print(ages["Ada"])        # 36
"Linus" in ages           # True - checks KEYS, not values
del ages["Linus"]
len(ages)                 # 2
```

Like sets, dicts use hashing, so lookups are fast no matter how big the
dict is. Keys must be immutable (str, int, tuple); values can be anything.

> **Pitfall:** `ages["Bob"]` for a missing key raises `KeyError`. Use
> `ages.get("Bob")` (gives `None`) or `ages.get("Bob", 0)` for a default.

### Counting

The most common dict job of all:

```python
counts = {}
for w in words:
    counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1
```

`get(w, 0)` returns 0 the first time a word is seen, so no special case is
needed.

### Looping

```python
for name in ages:                  # keys
for age in ages.values():          # values
for name, age in ages.items():     # both - the usual choice
```

Since Python 3.7 a dict remembers **insertion order**, so loops visit keys
in the order they were first added. To loop in another order, sort:
`for k in sorted(d)` (by key) or
`sorted(d.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1])` (by value - see the lambda
lesson).

> **Pitfall:** don't add or remove keys while looping over the same dict -
> loop over `list(d)` if you must.

examples.explain: `in` looks at keys; .get avoids a KeyError for missing keys.

title: Defining Functions
summary: def, parameters, return values and default arguments.
body:
A **function** packages code under a name so you can reuse it and test it
on its own:

```python
def area(width, height):
    return width * height

print(area(3, 4))     # 12
```

- `def` starts the definition; `width, height` are **parameters**.
- `return` hands a value back to the caller and **ends** the function.
- Calling `area(3, 4)` passes the **arguments** 3 and 4.

### return is not print

> **Pitfall:** a function that only `print`s gives back `None`. If the
> caller needs the value (to add it, compare it, store it), you must
> `return` it. A function with no `return` returns `None`.

### Default and keyword arguments

```python
def greet(name, greeting="Hello"):
    return f"{greeting}, {name}!"

greet("Ada")                    # 'Hello, Ada!'
greet("Ada", "Hi")              # 'Hi, Ada!'
greet(greeting="Hey", name="Bo")  # keywords: any order
```

Parameters with defaults must come after those without.

> **Pitfall: mutable defaults.** The default value is created **once**,
> when `def` runs - not on every call:
>
> ```python
> def add(item, bag=[]):    # BAD: one shared list
>     bag.append(item)
>     return bag
> ```
>
> Every call without `bag` reuses the same list, so items pile up. Use
> `bag=None` and inside write `if bag is None: bag = []`.

Good functions do **one thing**, have a descriptive verb name
(`count_vowels`, `is_prime`) and get everything they need through
parameters.

examples.title: return a value
examples.code:
def area(width, height):
    return width * height

def show_area(width, height):
    print(width * height)

a = area(3, 4)
b = show_area(3, 4)
print("a =", a, "b =", b)
examples.explain: show_area prints but returns None, so b is None.

title: Scope
summary: Local vs global names, UnboundLocalError, and why to pass values in and out.
body:
Names created inside a function are **local**: they exist only while the
function runs and are invisible outside.

```python
def f():
    secret = 42
f()
print(secret)     # NameError
```

A function **can read** a global (module-level) name:

```python
rate = 0.25
def tax(price):
    return price * rate     # fine: just reading
```

### The assignment rule

If a function **assigns** to a name anywhere in its body, Python treats
that name as local for the **whole** function:

```python
total = 0
def add(x):
    total = total + x   # UnboundLocalError!
```

Python decided `total` is local (because of the assignment), so reading it
on the right-hand side fails - the local has no value yet.

You *could* write `global total` inside the function, but that is usually a
design smell: hidden shared state makes functions hard to test and reason
about. The clean fix is to **pass values in and return results out**:

```python
def add(total, x):
    return total + x

total = add(total, 5)
```

> **Mutating vs assigning:** `items.append(x)` inside a function changes a
> global list *without* any `global` keyword, because you are not
> re-assigning the name - you are calling a method on the object it points
> to. Convenient, but also a source of surprises.

For a function nested inside another, `nonlocal name` lets the inner one
re-assign the outer one's variable - you will rarely need it.

Rule of thumb: a function should depend only on its parameters and
communicate only through its return value.

examples.code:

    return price * rate
print(tax(100))
examples.explain: Reading is fine; Python finds rate in the global scope.

examples.explain: The assignment makes total local, so the right-hand side has nothing to read.

examples.explain: No globals needed: the function is easy to test in isolation.

title: lambda & sorted(key=...)
summary: Functions are values: pass them to sorted, max and min to customise ordering.
body:
In Python a function is a value like any other - you can store it in a
variable or pass it to another function:

```python
def by_length(word):
    return len(word)

sorted(["kiwi", "fig", "banana"], key=by_length)
# ['fig', 'kiwi', 'banana']
```

`key=` tells `sorted` to compare items by `key(item)` instead of the item
itself. `min`, `max` and `list.sort` accept `key=` too.

### lambda

For tiny one-off functions, a **lambda** saves you the `def`:

```python
sorted(words, key=lambda w: len(w))
max(people, key=lambda p: p[1])      # tuple with the biggest score
```

`lambda args: expression` - no `return`, no statements, just one
expression. If it grows complicated, use a normal `def` with a name.

### Sorting by several things

Return a **tuple** from the key. Tuples compare element by element, so this
sorts by length and breaks ties alphabetically:

```python
sorted(words, key=lambda w: (len(w), w))
```

To sort one part descending and another ascending, negate the number:
`key=lambda p: (-p[1], p[0])` for `(name, score)` pairs.

`reverse=True` flips the whole order. Python's sort is **stable**: items
with equal keys keep their original relative order.

> **Pitfall:** `key=len()` calls `len` immediately (with no argument) and
> fails. Pass the function itself: `key=len`.

> **Pitfall:** sorting numbers that are still strings: `sorted(["10", "9"])`
> gives `['10', '9']` (alphabetical). Convert first, or use `key=int`.

examples.code:
words = ["kiwi", "fig", "banana", "apple"]
print(sorted(words))
print(sorted(words, key=len))
print(sorted(words, key=lambda w: w[-1]))
print(max(words, key=len))
examples.explain: key=len passes the built-in len function; lambda sorts by last letter.

examples.title: Multi-key sort
examples.code:
people = [("Bob", 91), ("Ada", 85), ("Al", 91)]
print(sorted(people, key=lambda p: p[1], reverse=True))
print(sorted(people, key=lambda p: (-p[1], p[0])))
examples.explain: Negate the score for descending; the name ascending breaks ties.

print(sorted(vals))
print(sorted(vals, key=int))

title: Recursion
summary: Functions that call themselves: base case, recursive case, and the call stack.
body:
A **recursive** function solves a problem by calling itself on a *smaller*
version of the same problem:

```python
def factorial(n):
    if n == 0:              # base case: answer known directly
        return 1
    return n * factorial(n - 1)   # recursive case: smaller problem
```

Every recursive function needs:

1. a **base case** that stops the recursion, and
2. a **recursive case** that moves *towards* the base case.

Forget either and you get infinite recursion, which Python stops with a
`RecursionError` after about 1000 nested calls.

### How it runs

Each call waits on a **call stack** until the inner call returns:
`factorial(3)` -> `3 * factorial(2)` -> `3 * 2 * factorial(1)` -> ... -> `6`.

> **Pitfall:** Python's default depth limit (~1000) is low. Recursing once
> per element of a 100 000-item list will crash; use a loop there, or
> `sys.setrecursionlimit` with care.

### Where recursion shines

Problems that branch naturally - trees, nested structures, generating all
combinations:

```python
def binary(prefix, n):
    if n == 0:
        print(prefix)
        return
    binary(prefix + "0", n - 1)
    binary(prefix + "1", n - 1)
```

### Memoisation

Naive Fibonacci recomputes the same values exponentially many times. Cache
results with `functools.lru_cache` and it becomes instant:

```python
from functools import lru_cache

@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def fib(n):
    return n if n < 2 else fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)
```

This "recursion + cache" idea is the doorway to dynamic programming.

examples.title: Factorial
examples.explain: Each call handles one n and delegates the rest to a smaller call.

examples.title: Memoised Fibonacci
examples.explain: Without the cache fib(90) would take longer than the age of the universe.

title: Comprehensions
summary: Build lists, sets and dicts in one readable line.
body:
You have written this loop many times:

```python
squares = []
for x in range(10):
    if x % 2 == 0:
        squares.append(x * x)
```

A **list comprehension** says the same in one line:

```python
squares = [x * x for x in range(10) if x % 2 == 0]
```

Read it left to right as "**x squared, for each x in range(10), if x is
even**". The pattern is `[expression for item in iterable if condition]`;
the `if` part is optional.

### Other flavours

```python
lengths = {w: len(w) for w in words}       # dict comprehension
first_letters = {w[0] for w in words}      # set comprehension
total = sum(x * x for x in nums)           # generator expression
```

A **generator expression** (round brackets, or none inside a function
call) produces values one at a time without building a list - ideal for
`sum`, `max`, `any`, `all`.

```python
any(n < 0 for n in nums)    # is there a negative?
all(c.isdigit() for c in s) # is s all digits?
```

### if/else inside

A filter `if` goes at the **end**. To *transform* with a choice, put a
conditional expression at the **front**:

```python
["even" if x % 2 == 0 else "odd" for x in nums]
```

Nested loops read in the same order as normal loops:
`[(r, c) for r in range(3) for c in range(3)]`.

> **Pitfall:** comprehensions are for *building* collections. If you only
> want side effects (printing), use a plain `for` loop. And if a
> comprehension needs two lines to read, a loop is probably clearer.

examples.title: Loop vs comprehension
examples.explain: Both produce the same list; the comprehension is shorter and idiomatic.

print({w: len(w) for w in words})
print(sorted({w[0] for w in words}))
print(sum(len(w) for w in words), any(len(w) > 5 for w in words))

print(["even" if x % 2 == 0 else "odd" for x in nums])
print([x for x in nums if x > 0])
print([(r, c) for r in range(2) for c in range(3)])

title: enumerate & zip
summary: Loop with an index, or over several sequences side by side.
body:
Beginners often write `for i in range(len(names)):` and then use
`names[i]`. Python has two helpers that make such loops cleaner and less
error-prone.

### enumerate - index and item together

```python
for i, name in enumerate(names):
    print(i, name)
```

Need numbering from 1 (for rankings, line numbers)? Pass `start=1`:
`enumerate(names, start=1)`.

### zip - walk sequences in parallel

```python
names = ["Ada", "Bo", "Cy"]
scores = [91, 78, 85]
for name, score in zip(names, scores):
    print(name, score)
```

`zip` pairs the first items, then the second items, and so on. Useful
tricks:

```python
dict(zip(names, scores))          # {'Ada': 91, 'Bo': 78, 'Cy': 85}
for a, b in zip(nums, nums[1:]):  # neighbouring pairs
    ...
```

> **Pitfall:** `zip` stops at the **shortest** input and silently drops the
> rest. If the lengths should match, `zip(a, b, strict=True)` (Python 3.10+)
> raises an error when they don't.

Both `enumerate` and `zip` are **lazy**: they produce pairs on demand
instead of building a list. Wrap them in `list()` if you want to print or
reuse the pairs.

Combining them is common: `for i, (a, b) in enumerate(zip(xs, ys)):` -
note the parentheses that unpack the inner pair.

examples.explain: No range(len(...)) needed; start=1 shifts the numbering.

#2 Bo

title: Counter, defaultdict & deque
summary: Three power tools from the collections module.
body:
The standard library's `collections` module has ready-made containers
for jobs you would otherwise code by hand.

### Counter - counting made trivial

```python
from collections import Counter
c = Counter("mississippi")
c["s"]              # 4
c["z"]              # 0 - missing keys count as zero, no KeyError
c.most_common(2)    # [('i', 4), ('s', 4)]
```

`Counter(words)` replaces the whole `counts.get(w, 0) + 1` loop.
`most_common` sorts by count; ties keep the order in which items were first
seen.

### defaultdict - dicts with automatic defaults

```python
from collections import defaultdict
groups = defaultdict(list)
for w in words:
    groups[w[0]].append(w)     # no "if key not in groups" needed
```

`defaultdict(list)` creates an empty list the first time a key is used;
`defaultdict(int)` starts at 0. You pass the *function* (`list`, `int`),
not a value.

### deque - a fast double-ended queue

```python
from collections import deque
q = deque([1, 2, 3])
q.append(4)        # right end
q.appendleft(0)    # left end
q.popleft()        # 0  - fast!
```

> **Pitfall:** `list.pop(0)` shifts every remaining element, so a queue
> built on a list gets slow with many items. `deque.popleft()` is
> constant-time - use it for queues and breadth-first search.

`deque(maxlen=3)` keeps only the last 3 items - perfect for "recent
history" windows.

examples.code:

c = Counter("mississippi")
print(c)
print(c["s"], c["z"])
print(c.most_common(2))

for x in range(6):
    recent.append(x)

title: math & itertools
summary: Ready-made maths functions and combinatorics generators.
body:
### The math module

```python
import math
math.sqrt(2)         # 1.4142...
math.isqrt(17)       # 4 - exact integer square root
math.gcd(12, 18)     # 6
math.lcm(4, 6)       # 12
math.factorial(5)    # 120
math.comb(5, 2)      # 10 - ways to choose 2 of 5
math.floor(2.7), math.ceil(2.1)   # 2, 3
math.pi, math.inf
```

> **Pitfall:** `int(math.sqrt(n))` can be off by one for huge `n` because
> of float rounding. Use `math.isqrt(n)` for exact integer roots.

### itertools - loops you don't have to write

```python
from itertools import combinations, permutations, product, accumulate

list(combinations("ABC", 2))   # [('A','B'), ('A','C'), ('B','C')]
list(permutations("AB"))       # [('A','B'), ('B','A')]
list(product([0, 1], repeat=2))  # (0,0) (0,1) (1,0) (1,1)
list(accumulate([1, 2, 3, 4]))   # [1, 3, 6, 10] - running totals
```

- `combinations(items, k)` - order doesn't matter, no repeats.
- `permutations(items, k)` - order matters.
- `product(a, b)` - every pairing, like nested loops.

These are **lazy** iterators and their output grows explosively:
`permutations(range(10))` has 3 628 800 items. They are perfect for small
brute-force searches, but check the count first (`math.comb`,
`math.factorial`) before looping.

Both modules are written in C, so they are much faster than equivalent
hand-written Python loops.

import math
print(math.sqrt(2), math.isqrt(17))
print(math.gcd(12, 18), math.lcm(4, 6))
print(math.factorial(5), math.comb(5, 2))
print(math.floor(2.7), math.ceil(2.1), round(math.pi, 4))
examples.explain: isqrt gives an exact integer; comb counts combinations.

title: Heaps with heapq
summary: Always grab the smallest item fast: priority queues in Python.
body:
Sometimes you repeatedly need **the smallest item** of a changing
collection - the next event, the cheapest task, the closest node. Sorting
after every change is slow. A **heap** keeps a list arranged so the
smallest item is always at index 0 and both inserting and removing take
only `O(log n)` steps.

```python
import heapq
h = []
heapq.heappush(h, 5)
heapq.heappush(h, 1)
heapq.heappush(h, 3)
h[0]                  # 1 - peek at the smallest
heapq.heappop(h)      # 1 - remove the smallest
```

`heapq.heapify(lst)` turns an existing list into a heap in place, in
linear time.

> **Pitfall:** the list is *heap-ordered*, not sorted. `print(h)` may show
> `[1, 5, 3]`. Only `h[0]` is guaranteed to be the minimum.

### Max-heaps

`heapq` only does **min**-heaps. For the largest first, push negated
values: `heappush(h, -x)` and negate again when you pop.

### Priorities

Push tuples `(priority, item)`: tuples compare by the first element, so the
smallest priority comes out first.

```python
heapq.heappush(tasks, (2, "write"))
heapq.heappush(tasks, (1, "plan"))
heapq.heappop(tasks)   # (1, 'plan')
```

For a one-off "top k", `heapq.nsmallest(k, data)` and
`heapq.nlargest(k, data)` are simpler than writing the loop.

Heaps power Dijkstra's shortest paths, event simulations and greedy
algorithms like "always merge the two smallest".

examples.title: Push and pop
examples.code:
import heapq
h = []
for x in [5, 1, 8, 3, 2]:
    heapq.heappush(h, x)
print("heap list:", h)
print([heapq.heappop(h) for _ in range(5)])
examples.explain: The internal list isn't sorted, but pops come out in order.

examples.title: Max-heap and top-k
examples.code:
import heapq
nums = list(map(int, input().split()))
h = [-x for x in nums]
heapq.heapify(h)
print("largest:", -heapq.heappop(h))
print(heapq.nsmallest(3, nums), heapq.nlargest(2, nums))
examples.explain: Negating turns a min-heap into a max-heap.

examples.title: Priority queue
examples.code:
import heapq
tasks = []
heapq.heappush(tasks, (2, "write code"))
heapq.heappush(tasks, (1, "plan"))
heapq.heappush(tasks, (3, "test"))
while tasks:
    prio, name = heapq.heappop(tasks)
    print(prio, name)
examples.explain: Tuples are compared by priority first.

challenge.prompt: Ropes. The input is a line of positive integer rope lengths. Joining two ropes of lengths `a` and `b` costs `a + b` and produces one rope of that length. Join all ropes into one with the **minimum total cost** (always join the two shortest) and print that cost. A single rope costs `0`.
